young.html: For parents: Cousin Bette is a novel for adults, about grown-ups' bad choices, broken promises and ruin. The young readers' path talks only about its main theme, envy, which children understand well.
Honoré de Balzac (say BAL-zak) was a French writer who drank huge amounts of coffee and wrote almost ninety novels about life in France. He wanted to describe a whole society, rich and poor.

Cousin Bette is about a poor cousin who smiles and helps her rich relatives, while secretly she is jealous of them, and her jealousy grows and grows until it causes great harm. Balzac shows how a small, hidden feeling can become dangerous if it is never faced.

young.html: The green-eyed monster. Envy means wanting what someone else has and feeling bad that they have it. Talk together: when have you felt envy? What helped it go away? Make a list of three things to do instead of letting envy grow, like telling someone, counting your own good things, or being glad for the other person.

full.html: Honoré de Balzac (1799–1850) wrote at a furious pace, often through the night, to pay off his debts. He gathered his novels and stories, around ninety in all, into one great series, The Human Comedy, in which characters reappear from book to book and together picture French society from peasants to bankers. Cousin Bette appeared as a newspaper serial in 1846; with Cousin Pons it forms a pair called Poor Relations. It is one of his last great novels.
Lisbeth Fischer, called Cousin Bette, comes from a peasant family in the Vosges. Her pretty cousin Adeline married a rising officer of Napoleon's army, Hector Hulot, who became a baron.

full.text: The family of the two brothers, who lived together, sacrificed the plain daughter to the pretty daughter, the bitter fruit to the dazzling flower. Lisbeth worked while Adeline was petted and indulged ...
full.author: Balzac

full.text: Thenceforth she gave up all idea of competition with her beautiful cousin, whose many superiorities she inwardly acknowledged; but envy lurked in her breast, as a germ of the plague lurks in a bale of woollen stuffs only to burst forth and ravage a city when the bale is opened.
full.author: Balzac

full.html: Bette has taken under her wing a young Polish sculptor in exile, Wenceslas Steinbock. When Adeline's daughter Hortense meets and marries him, Bette's buried envy turns into a plan for revenge. She allies herself with Valérie Marneffe, a scheming young wife who entangles Baron Hulot and the rich Crevel and drains their money. The baron's weakness leads him into debt, disgrace and the ruin of others. Through it all Adeline, patient and pious, keeps forgiving.

full.html: Balzac is a founder of literary realism. He describes rooms, clothes, debts and prices in great detail, because he believed people's money and surroundings shape their souls. Cousin Bette shows a society in which money and appearances rule, and in which hidden passions, envy most of all, do more harm than open crimes.

Readers have long argued about Balzac's view. Some see him as a moralist who shows vice destroying itself and goodness, in Adeline, enduring; others see a coolly scientific observer more interested in how passions work than in judging them. Balzac himself, in his foreword to the Human Comedy, compared himself to a naturalist classifying species.

Seeing Bette as a simple villain. Balzac makes us understand her: a lifetime of being overlooked, and pride that will not admit it. That does not excuse what she does, but it makes the book a study of how resentment grows.

items: Dante had already pictured envy as a sin that blinds; Balzac shows it working in a modern city.
Dickens and George Eliot, later in this era, also show families undone by money, debt and secrets.
Engels, Marx's partner, wrote that he learned more about French society from Balzac than from all the historians and economists.
Tolstoy and Dostoevsky carried Balzac's realism into Russia.
Why is hidden envy more dangerous than open anger?
Can understanding why someone does wrong be different from excusing it?
Is forgiveness like Adeline's always wise?
How much do money and surroundings shape a person's character?

questions: What is the difference between envy and wanting to do well?
Why do you think Bette hid her feelings for so long?
Adeline forgave again and again. When is forgiving the right thing, and when does someone need to change first?
How can a family make sure no one feels left out or less loved?
Balzac described rooms and money in great detail. Why might that help tell a story?
